# Why this run exists

Study 1 scores a word by its **first subword** under a causal LM. That was a
convention adopted without a test, and it makes a word's surprisal depend on how
its tokenizer cuts the word up. The more pieces a word is cut into, the more
continuations its first piece sums over, and the cheaper the word looks. The
alternative, summing a word's subword surprisals, recovers the word's actual
information content by the chain rule and does not have that property.

Two exposures follow, and both land on claims Study 1 actually makes.

1. **Cross-model ranking.** The eleven models do not share a tokenizer, so the
   deflation is not constant across the configurations being ranked.
2. **Concurrent validity.** Fertility is a property of the writing, not only of
   the tokenizer. Misspellings, non-target morphology and rare vocabulary all
   split into more pieces, and all are more frequent in lower-proficiency
   writing. If fertility tracks proficiency, then part of what the measure
   correlates with is how the tokenizer treats the text.

Neither claim needs a language model to check, only its tokenizer, so this runs
on both corpora in full rather than on a subsample. `fertility.py` writes the
per-essay table this report reads.

**What this report is not.** It does not estimate what the measure would be under
a different aggregation convention. It establishes whether the question is worth
the GPU time, and if so, where the exposure sits.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

set.seed(42)
N_BOOT <- 2000
D_FLAG <- 0.10   # Williamson et al. (2012) flag threshold, as in the main analysis
FOCAL  <- "olmo2-1b"   # the selected configuration's model, at window 8

find_results <- function() {
  d <- normalizePath(getwd())
  for (i in 1:6) {
    cand <- file.path(d, "results", "predictability")
    if (dir.exists(cand)) return(cand)
    d <- dirname(d)
  }
  stop("results/predictability not found — run sensitivity/fertility.py first")
}
RESULTS <- find_results()

for (hp in c("../_viz_helpers.R", "src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")) {
  if (file.exists(hp)) { source(hp); break }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: load
fert <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "fertility_by_essay.csv.gz"),
                 col_types = cols(text_id = col_character(),
                                  l1 = col_character(), level = col_character(),
                                  .default = col_guess()))
toks <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "fertility_tokenizers.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# One row per essay per *tokenizer*; the model-keyed rows are replays of these.
uniq <- fert |>
  distinct(corpus, text_id, tokenizer_group, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    family      = factor(model_family(tokenizer_group), levels = FAMILY_LEVELS),
    split_rate  = n_split2_alpha / n_words_alpha,
    split3_rate = n_split3_alpha / n_words_alpha,
    straddle_rate  = n_straddle / n_subwords,
    unaligned_rate = n_unaligned_alpha / n_words_alpha
  )
ell <- filter(uniq, corpus == "ellipse")
toe <- filter(uniq, corpus == "toefl11") |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = LEVEL_LEVELS))
```

# Section 1 — Eleven models, six tokenizers

Before anything else, how many distinct tokenizers are actually in the matrix.
Two models that share one cannot differ from each other for tokenization reasons,
which bounds how much of the cross-model ranking this can touch.

```{r}
#| label: tokenizer-groups
toks |>
  group_by(tokenizer_group) |>
  summarise(models = paste(model, collapse = ", "),
            vocab_size = first(vocab_size), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(vocab_size) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Tokenizer", "Models sharing it", "Vocab size"))
```

Six. The base/instruct pairs share a tokenizer, as do `gpt2`/`gpt2-xl` and the
two ModernBERT and OLMo-2 checkpoints. So of the fifteen within-window model
contrasts that matter to the selection rule, five are tokenizer-identical by
construction and cannot be explained by this.

# Section 2 — How often the question even arises

A word only exposes the convention if it is split into more than one piece. If
almost nothing splits, first-subword and summed surprisal agree on almost every
word and the rest of this report is about a rare event.

Fertility below is subwords per **alphabetic** spaCy token, which excludes
punctuation and numerals. The all-token version is in the table too.

```{r}
#| label: fertility-desc
bind_rows(ell, toe) |>
  group_by(corpus, tokenizer_group) |>
  summarise(fertility_alpha = mean(fertility_alpha),
            fertility_all   = mean(fertility),
            split_rate      = mean(split_rate),
            split3_rate     = mean(split3_rate), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(corpus, fertility_alpha) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Corpus", "Tokenizer", "Subwords/word (alpha)",
                      "Subwords/token (all)", "Words split ≥2", "Words split ≥3"))
```

Fertility runs about 1.02 on ELLIPSE and 1.04–1.06 on TOEFL 11, so roughly two
to four per cent of words split at all. The convention is therefore a rare event
in frequency terms, and a first reading is that it cannot matter much.

That reading is wrong for the reason the next two sections give. The words that
split are not a random two per cent. They are the misspelled, the morphologically
unusual and the rare, which is to say the words that carry most of the
proficiency signal, and they carry far more surprisal each than an average word.
Rarity in frequency and smallness in effect are not the same thing.

# Section 3 — Fertility tracks proficiency

ELLIPSE first, against the holistic score, per tokenizer.

```{r}
#| label: ellipse-r
ell_r <- ell |>
  group_by(tokenizer_group) |>
  summarise(
    r_fertility = cor(fertility_alpha, overall),
    r_split     = cor(split_rate, overall),
    rho         = cor(fertility_alpha, overall, method = "spearman"),
    n           = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(r_fertility)

ell_r |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & !n, \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Tokenizer", "r (fertility, holistic)", "r (split rate, holistic)",
                      "Spearman rho", "n"))
```

Every tokenizer correlates with the holistic score at about `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(abs(ell_r$r_fertility)))`
in magnitude, negatively: more proficient writing splits less. For scale, the
highest-validity configuration class in the main analysis reaches mean
`|r|` = .627. A quantity computed with no language model at all, from the
tokenizer alone, reaches roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(abs(ell_r$r_fertility)) / 0.627)`
per cent of that.

TOEFL 11 has only three proficiency levels, so the same relationship shows up as
a level contrast.

```{r}
#| label: toefl-level
toe |>
  group_by(tokenizer_group) |>
  summarise(
    low = mean(fertility_alpha[level == "low"]),
    medium = mean(fertility_alpha[level == "medium"]),
    high = mean(fertility_alpha[level == "high"]),
    d_low_high = (low - high) / sd(fertility_alpha),
    r_level = cor(fertility_alpha, as.integer(level)), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(d_low_high)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Tokenizer", "Low", "Medium", "High",
                      "d (low − high)", "r with level"))
```

The gap between low and high is around one standard deviation for every
tokenizer. This is a large effect on a variable that is supposed to be an
implementation detail.

In the figure below the OLMo-2 and Qwen2.5 series sit on top of each other and
only the upper one is visible. That is not an artefact. The two tokenizers agree
on fertility to four decimal places on both corpora despite differing in vocabulary
size by a factor of one and a half, which is a useful reminder that vocabulary
size is a poor proxy for how a tokenizer treats learner writing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fertility-proficiency
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
# Both corpora on one panel row: the criterion is a 0.5-step holistic score on
# ELLIPSE and a three-level band on TOEFL 11, so the facets take free x scales
# and the bands enter as an ordered factor rather than a shared numeric axis.
band_means <- bind_rows(
  ell |>
    filter(overall >= 1.5, overall <= 4.5) |>
    transmute(family, panel = "ELLIPSE (holistic score)",
              band = factor(format(overall, nsmall = 1)), fertility_alpha),
  toe |>
    transmute(family, panel = "TOEFL 11 (proficiency level)",
              band = factor(as.character(level), levels = LEVEL_LEVELS),
              fertility_alpha)
  ) |>
  group_by(panel, family, band) |>
  summarise(m = mean(fertility_alpha),
            se = sd(fertility_alpha) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop")

p_fert <- ggplot(band_means, aes(band, m, colour = family, group = family)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = FAMILY_COLORS, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Subwords per word", colour = "Tokenizer",
       title = "Fertility falls as proficiency rises, under every tokenizer",
       subtitle = "Essay means with 95% intervals. Alphabetic tokens only.") +
  theme_study1(base_size = 11)
p_fert
save_fig(p_fert, "fertility_by_proficiency", width = 9, height = 4.2)
```

# Section 4 — Fertility displaces L1 groups

The main analysis measures fairness as max `|d|` across the eleven L1 groups,
computed within proficiency strata and weighted by focal-group size. Running that
same statistic on fertility asks how much cross-L1 displacement the tokenizer
contributes before any model is involved.

```{r}
#| label: dif
col_var <- function(x) apply(x, 2, var)

group_d <- function(y, l1, level, strata = LEVEL_LEVELS) {
  groups <- sort(unique(l1))
  vapply(groups, function(g) {
    num <- 0; wsum <- 0
    for (s in strata) {
      in_s <- level == s
      a <- y[in_s & l1 == g]; b <- y[in_s & l1 != g]
      n1 <- length(a); n2 <- length(b)
      if (n1 < 2L || n2 < 2L) next
      sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var(a) + (n2 - 1) * var(b)) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
      num <- num + n1 * (mean(a) - mean(b)) / sp
      wsum <- wsum + n1
    }
    num / wsum
  }, numeric(1))
}

dif <- toe |>
  group_by(tokenizer_group) |>
  group_modify(\(d, k) {
    dd <- group_d(d$fertility_alpha, d$l1, as.character(d$level))
    tibble(max_abs_d = max(abs(dd)), worst_l1 = names(dd)[which.max(abs(dd))],
           n_flag = sum(abs(dd) >= D_FLAG))
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(max_abs_d)

dif |>
  mutate(max_abs_d = round(max_abs_d, 3)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Tokenizer", "max |d|", "Worst L1", "Groups over flag (of 11)"))
```

Fertility alone displaces L1 groups by max `|d|` of
`r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(dif$max_abs_d), max(dif$max_abs_d))`, and the
worst group is Arabic under every tokenizer. The selected configuration
`olmo2-1b/8` has a max `|d|` of .42 on the measure itself, on Telugu.

Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions. The displacement the
tokenizer produces is *larger* than the displacement the finished measure shows,
which is not reassuring. But it falls on a different group, so the measure's
unfairness is not simply fertility passing through. Arabic writing is cut into
more pieces than anyone else's and the measure does not flag Arabic hardest, so
whatever the tokenizer is doing to Arabic is being partly absorbed somewhere
between the pieces and the essay score.

# Section 5 — How much of the validity runs through this channel

The direct question. Take the main analysis's own ELLIPSE validity coefficient at
window 8, and partial fertility out of it. What survives is the part of the
correlation that is not shared with how the tokenizer cut the text up.

```{r}
#| label: partial
ell_long <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ellipse_long.csv.gz"),
                     col_types = cols(window = col_character(),
                                      text_id = col_character())) |>
  filter(window == "8") |>
  inner_join(fert |> filter(corpus == "ellipse") |>
               select(text_id, model, fertility_alpha),
             by = c("text_id", "model"))

partial_r <- function(x, y, z) {
  rxy <- cor(x, y); rxz <- cor(x, z); ryz <- cor(y, z)
  (rxy - rxz * ryz) / sqrt((1 - rxz^2) * (1 - ryz^2))
}

pr <- ell_long |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(
    abs_r      = abs(cor(mean_surprisal_bits, overall)),
    abs_r_part = abs(partial_r(mean_surprisal_bits, overall, fertility_alpha)),
    r_surp_fert = cor(mean_surprisal_bits, fertility_alpha),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(retained = abs_r_part / abs_r,
         rank_before = rank(-abs_r), rank_after = rank(-abs_r_part)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs_r))

pr |>
  mutate(across(c(abs_r, abs_r_part, r_surp_fert, retained), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  select(model, abs_r, abs_r_part, retained, r_surp_fert, rank_before, rank_after) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model (window 8)", "|r|", "|r| · fertility held",
                      "Retained", "r (surprisal, fertility)", "Rank before", "Rank after"))
```

```{r}
#| label: boot-drop
wide <- ell_long |>
  select(text_id, model, mean_surprisal_bits, fertility_alpha, overall) |>
  arrange(model, text_id)
ids <- unique(wide$text_id)
mods <- unique(wide$model)
S <- matrix(wide$mean_surprisal_bits, nrow = length(ids), dimnames = list(NULL, mods))
F <- matrix(wide$fertility_alpha,     nrow = length(ids), dimnames = list(NULL, mods))
y <- wide$overall[wide$model == mods[1]]

drop_boot <- replicate(N_BOOT, {
  i <- sample.int(length(ids), replace = TRUE)
  yb <- y[i]
  vapply(seq_along(mods), function(k) {
    x <- S[i, k]; z <- F[i, k]
    abs(cor(x, yb)) - abs(partial_r(x, yb, z))
  }, numeric(1))
})
rownames(drop_boot) <- mods

boot_tbl <- tibble(
  model = mods,
  drop  = pr$abs_r[match(mods, pr$model)] - pr$abs_r_part[match(mods, pr$model)],
  lo    = apply(drop_boot, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  hi    = apply(drop_boot, 1, quantile, 0.975)) |>
  arrange(desc(drop))

boot_tbl |>
  mutate(across(c(drop, lo, hi), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model (window 8)", "Drop in |r|", "2.5%", "97.5%"),
        caption = paste0("Essay-level bootstrap, ", N_BOOT, " resamples."))
```

The coefficient falls, and the interval on the fall excludes zero everywhere, so
the channel is real rather than noise. It is also small. The selected
configuration goes from
`r sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", pr$abs_r[pr$model == FOCAL], pr$abs_r_part[pr$model == FOCAL])`,
retaining `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pr$retained[pr$model == FOCAL])` per cent of
its validity with fertility held constant.

The ranking is what the selection rule actually consumes, and it barely moves:
`r sum(pr$rank_before != pr$rank_after)` of `r nrow(pr)` models change rank, none
by more than one place. The two masked models stay at the bottom of the ordering
before and after.

One detail in that table is not about the tokenizer. The two masked models show
the strongest coupling between surprisal and fertility
(`r sprintf("%.2f", max(pr$r_surp_fert))` for `bert-base`, against
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(pr$r_surp_fert))` at the other end). That is the
signature of a separate problem: the masked path in
`features.predictability` averages over a word's subwords rather than summing
them, so a masked model's word score is information *density* per subword, and
fertility is its denominator. The causal path scores one subword and has no such
denominator. The two architectures are not measuring the same thing, and that is
a defect to fix rather than a result to interpret.

```{r}
#| label: fig-partial
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
p_part <- pr |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = rev(pr$model[order(pr$abs_r)])),
         family = factor(model_family(as.character(model)), levels = FAMILY_LEVELS)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = model)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = abs_r_part, xend = abs_r, yend = model),
               colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(x = abs_r, colour = family), size = 2.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = abs_r_part, colour = family), size = 2.6, shape = 21,
             fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = FAMILY_COLORS, drop = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "ELLIPSE validity  |r|", y = NULL, colour = "Family",
       title = "Validity with and without the fertility channel",
       subtitle = "Filled = as reported; open = fertility held constant. Window 8.") +
  theme_study1(base_size = 11)
p_part
save_fig(p_part, "fertility_partial_validity", width = 7.5, height = 4.6)
```

# Section 6 — Whether the spans are even right

Any move away from first-subword needs a word's subword span to be correct.
Two diagnostics bear on that, both cheap byproducts of the measurement.

`n_straddle` counts subwords crossing a spaCy token boundary, where no word-level
aggregation can recover the word's probability exactly. `n_unaligned_alpha`
counts alphabetic words receiving no subword of their own, which is the
alignment failure that matters, because `features.predictability` builds a word's
span as the gap to the *next aligned word* and silently folds an unaligned word
into its predecessor.

```{r}
#| label: alignment
bind_rows(ell, toe) |>
  group_by(corpus, tokenizer_group) |>
  summarise(straddle_rate = mean(straddle_rate),
            unaligned_rate = mean(unaligned_rate),
            essays_with_unaligned = mean(n_unaligned_alpha > 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(corpus, desc(unaligned_rate)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Corpus", "Tokenizer", "Straddling subwords (per subword)",
                      "Unaligned alpha words (per word)", "Essays with ≥1"))
```

The rates are low but not zero, and they are concentrated: a small share of
essays carries them. Under the current first-subword convention this is
harmless, because only one subword index is ever read. It stops being harmless
the moment a word's span is summed over, and there is a second span defect that
these counts do not capture at all: `pairwise(..., add_extra = True)` gives the
final aligned word of every document a span of exactly one subword, so the last
word of every essay would be truncated under summing. A joint-probability run
should rebuild spans from the offset mapping rather than reuse `token_map`.

# Read-out

- Fertility is not an implementation detail. It correlates with ELLIPSE holistic
  score at about `|r|` = .28 and separates TOEFL 11 low from high by about one
  standard deviation, under all six tokenizers.
- It displaces L1 groups more than the finished measure does
  (max `|d|` up to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(dif$max_abs_d))` against .42), though
  on Arabic rather than on the Telugu the measure flags, so it is not the same
  unfairness travelling through.
- Despite that, the validity coefficient is not mainly riding on this channel.
  Holding fertility constant costs the selected configuration
  `r sprintf("%.3f", pr$abs_r[pr$model == FOCAL] - pr$abs_r_part[pr$model == FOCAL])`
  of its `|r|`, and the model ranking the selection rule reads is unchanged in
  substance.
- The six-tokenizer structure limits the blast radius further. Five of the
  within-window contrasts are tokenizer-identical and cannot move.

That combination is the argument for a bounded follow-up rather than a rerun.
The ranking that Study 1 reports does not appear to be a tokenization artefact,
which is the claim the chapter needs to defend. What remains open is the size of
the gap between first-subword and summed surprisal on the two-to-four per cent of
words that split, which this report cannot estimate because it never ran a model.
A subsample comparison at window 8 answers it, and the masked-path averaging
defect named in Section 5 should be fixed in the same pass, since until it is,
the masked and causal arms are not measuring the same construct.
